query_text: how do bacteriophages differ from antibiotics

content.text:
Bacteriophages (“phages”) and antibiotics both can be used to fight bacterial infections, but they work very differently.

| Feature | Bacteriophages | Antibiotics |
|---|---|---|
| **What they are** | Viruses that infect bacteria | Chemical drugs, natural or synthetic |
| **Target** | Usually very specific bacterial strains or species | Often broader: may affect many bacterial species |
| **How they kill bacteria** | Attach to bacteria, inject genetic material, replicate inside, and often burst the cell | Interfere with bacterial processes like cell-wall building, protein synthesis, DNA replication, or metabolism |
| **Effect on microbiome** | Usually less disruptive because they target specific bacteria | Can disrupt normal helpful bacteria, especially broad-spectrum antibiotics |
| **Resistance** | Bacteria can become phage-resistant, but phages can also evolve or be modified to match bacteria | Bacteria can become antibiotic-resistant through mutations or resistance genes |
| **Dosing behavior** | Can multiply at the infection site if the target bacteria are present | Do not reproduce; drug levels depend on dose, absorption, metabolism, and excretion |
| **Clinical use** | Still limited in many countries; often experimental or compassionate-use for resistant infections | Widely used, standardized, and regulated |
| **Specificity tradeoff** | Precision can be good, but the right phage must match the infection | Broad coverage can be useful before the exact bacterium is known, but may cause more collateral damage |

**In short:** antibiotics are chemical agents that broadly or selectively inhibit bacteria, while bacteriophages are bacteria-infecting viruses that usually target particular bacterial strains. Phages may be especially useful against antibiotic-resistant infections, but they are generally more personalized and less standardized than conventional antibiotics.
